title.en: Sources of water and the water cycle

text.en: Jyoti puts ice cubes in a steel glass and sees tiny water droplets on the outside. Where do they come from?

Water has three forms: liquid like rain, solid like ice and vapour like steam.
In the activity with ice cubes, the ice melts into water, and heated water turns to steam. Water can change form and return to liquid.
In the bag activity, a transparent bag with coloured water is sealed and put in the sun. The Sun's heat turns water into water vapour. When the vapour cools, it forms droplets that fall back down.
In nature heat from the Sun changes water from oceans and rivers into vapour. The vapour forms clouds, which come down as rain, snow and hail. The water goes back to rivers, lakes and oceans. This constant circular movement of water is called the water cycle.
When it rains, some water soaks into the soil and sinks through layers of soil and rock. The water stored deep underground is groundwater.
We dig wells, borewells, tube wells and handpumps to draw groundwater. In cities with many cemented surfaces rainwater cannot go into the ground easily, so groundwater is not recharged.
Open areas, soak pits, ponds, human-made lakes and more trees help rainwater go underground. Johads in Rajasthan are small earthen dams that collect rainwater and recharge groundwater.
Surface water in rivers, ponds and lakes is also a source of freshwater. Rivers begin in the mountains and flow downhill, following the shape of the land.

problem.en: Describe the water cycle in four steps.

text.en: The Sun heats water in oceans and rivers.
The vapour rises and cools into clouds.
Rain, snow or hail falls and flows back to rivers and oceans, or soaks in as groundwater.

prompt.en: Explain how the water cycle works.

requiredIdeas.en: Rain falls and returns to rivers and oceans

points.en: Water is liquid, solid or vapour.
The water cycle is the constant movement of water.
Groundwater is stored under the soil.
